content: Epiphora is a condition characterized by excessive tear production, which typically occurs as a result of irritation to the eye. It can also arise from inadequate drainage of the tear film, leading to tears overflowing onto the face instead of being properly drained through the nasolacrimal system. The causes of epiphora include ocular irritation and inflammation, such as trichiasis (misdirected eyelashes) and entropion (inward turning of the eyelid). Another common cause is obstruction of the tear outflow tract, which can occur at various anatomical locations, including ectropion (outward turning of the eyelid), punctal obstruction, canalicular blockage, or nasolacrimal duct obstruction. Obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct is often associated with aging, infections such as dacryocystitis, rhinitis, or, in neonates and infants, failure of the nasolacrimal duct to open properly. A less common cause of epiphora is paradoxical lacrimation, which results from abnormal regeneration of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) following Bell's palsy. In this condition, nerve fibers that originally innervated the salivary glands regenerate and instead connect to the lacrimal gland, leading to excessive tearing. This phenomenon is often triggered during eating, as the facial nerve also controls the muscles of mastication, and their activation inadvertently stimulates tear production. The diagnosis of epiphora is primarily clinical, based on the patient’s history and physical examination, including observation of the eyelids. Fluorescein dye testing can be employed to assess for punctal reflux by applying pressure to the canaliculi. The clinician evaluates for resistance or reflux as the dye is irrigated through the punctum into the nasal cavity. Management of epiphora depends on the underlying cause. If the condition is due to ectropion or entropion, surgical repair of the eyelid is indicated. Punctal irrigation is also necessary in some cases. In infants with nasolacrimal duct defects, a nasolacrimal duct probe is used to open the obstruction, and a tube may be placed for drainage, either temporarily (Crawford tube) or permanently (Jones tube). For more severe cases, a surgical procedure called dacryocystorhinostomy is performed. This involves creating a direct connection between the lacrimal sac and the nasal mucosa to restore proper tear drainage.
